reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors studied 16 patients with metastatic melanoma. At first glance, the sample size appears exceedingly small and if this association (OS and high TCR clonality) is true, it should be broadened to be truly representative of newly diagnosed patients to convince one that others can build upon these results. The limited information in the data summary is inadequate.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added more detailed clinical characteristics in Table 1 and analysed 3 additional independent cohorts (Tumeh 2014, Roh 2017, Amaria 2019) in new Figure 1e-j, confirming that high TIL/Tc clonality in pre-treatment biopsies correlated with benefit from therapy.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The median number of unique TCR sequences in each group is 10 which is dramatically lower than expected based on the literature. The low number of unique TCR clonotypes for each patient probably reflects a sampling bias or alternatively, a sequencing artifact due to their methodology. The authors should be more precise in their definition of a TCR clonotype and the primary sequencing data for all 16 subjects should be provided.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added explorative TCR repertoire analysis comparing RNA-Seq with targeted sequencing platforms, showing that although the number of unique clonotypes differed, overall calculated clonality did not. Reviewer #3 in round 2 maintained reservations about using RNA-Seq to infer TCR repertoire.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The high and low thresholds applied for the survival curve analyses need to be explained more explicitly in Methods.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified the cut-off methodology in Methods and noted that regression analyses retained TCR metrics as continuous variables to avoid cut-off bias.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Figure 1a-d: It would appear that in both melanoma cohorts, more patients tend to have low clonality. Is such a distribution to be expected? Is it then correct to deduce that a majority of metastatic melanoma patients should not receive PD1 blockade despite this being the standard treatment?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that categorisation into high/low clonality was needed only for Kaplan-Meier curves, and that all regression analyses retained TCR metrics as continuous covariates; also added context about anti-PD1 response rates (20-55%).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Comment 3 addressed the claim that TCR diversity is prognostic for OS in several other solid tumors. It is unclear how this observation made using TCGA samples is relevant to the melanoma work.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors argued the TCGA analysis demonstrates TIL diversity is prognostic in tumours not treated with immunotherapy, supporting that TIL clonality is a predictive biomarker specific to checkpoint blockade.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: Paper is borderline omics scope (TCR sequencing + clinical survival). Concerns predominantly about sample size and sequencing methodology. Reviewer #4 added in round 2 with only positive comments. Reviewer #3 round 2 maintained methodology concerns about RNA-Seq for TCR inference, which authors declined to fully address.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I do not see any methodological novelty in the development of the deep learning system, and yet the reported AUCs are much higher than reported by others. The average AUC in Table 2 is 0.999 with very tight confidence intervals in most cases. Can the authors validate their DLP on publicly available datasets for at least some of the predictions and report the performance for comparison? Two example public datasets for validating the referrable DR predictions are EyePACS Kaggle dataset and Messidor-2.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged that AUC can be over-optimistic with extreme class imbalance (ratios 0.7-4028.7), recommended F1 as more suitable, and validated on public datasets Messidor-2, IDRID, PALM, REFUGE achieving lower but acceptable performance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Line 466 What happens if a patient was imaged both before 2018 and after 2018. Do you discard such patients from the test set?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that 2,677 images (1,635 subjects) from the 2018 dataset were discarded if patients had been imaged before 2018; primary test set results were recalculated.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The external test sets were all DR, thus claiming that the performance on external datasets is perhaps overoptimistic.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors tested on REFUGE (glaucoma) and PALM (pathological myopia) public datasets in addition to DR datasets, showing weaker but acceptable generalization (F1 0.651 for optic nerve degeneration).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The 39 diseases are not really diseases but a mix of findings and diseases. Laser spots, silicone oil etc are more a consequence of treatment! There is expected to be a lot of overlap between the categories. It is not clear how this overlap was dealt with.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged the mix of diseases, findings, and conditions; added 'and conditions' to title; explained the multi-label classification using Binary Relevance to deal with class overlaps.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The ground truth labels were provided by 20 ophthalmologists in 10 teams of each a retina specialist and an ophthalmologist in training. Did the authors study how reproducible these 10 teams worked compared to each other and along their task (inter-grader and intra-grader reproducibility)?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added inter-grader agreement statistics in Supplementary Table 3.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The utility and accuracy of the heatmaps are unclear. There is not quantification of their ability to localize.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added quantitative analysis only for bigclass 10 (optic nerve degeneration), showing 100% (1,054 images) of heatmaps focused on optic disc areas; acknowledged quantitative evaluation was difficult across multiple diseases.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: Imaging modality (fundus photos) — formally out of MLGG core scope per CLAUDE.md, but concerns themselves are general ML methodology (class imbalance, label noise, split hygiene, external validation). Three reviewers, three rounds, all reviewers satisfied by final round.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The empirical evidence is subjective. First, it is based on three cytopathologists who are with limited justifications of the screening ability, which can lead to a serious bias. Second, the screening difficulty of the data used is missing, which makes me rather difficult to assess the effectiveness of this work.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified the standard cytopathology procedure of consensus by three cytopathologists, abandoned questionable annotations, and added data screening procedure description in Methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Whether cytology with automation will serve as a primary screening method for much of the world is increasingly doubtful. HPV testing is more sensitive as a first screen. The place of this AI-advance in a system dependent on HPV testing first is not clear, because the performance characteristics of the automated prescreen among HPV-positive women is not the subject of study.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors conducted a preliminary trial on 395 HPV-positive patients achieving 81.9% specificity and 79.3% sensitivity with 0.890 AUC (lower than general population performance); added discussion that triage in HPV-positive women requires retraining.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The only contribution is the dataset, but it will not be publicly available.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors stated WSI and annotation data are not publicly available due to patient privacy in cooperative hospitals; provided source data for figures and a small sample of slides for software testing.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: To achieve 100% sensitivity (if that is the goal) two thirds of HPV positive women would be referred. I think the work is interesting, but the performance for triage is not established as sufficient for management of HPV-positive women.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: No further author response captured in round 2 — reviewer concern persisted but paper accepted.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: Imaging modality (WSI cervical cytology) — out of MLGG core scope. Methodology concerns are general. Reviewer #2 round 2 maintained reservations about HPV-positive subgroup performance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper relates to several different but easily-confused concepts: 'ECG-age', 'chronological age', 'predicted ECG-age', and 'predicted chronological age'. The deep neural network is actually trained with 'chronological age', then the predictions should be called 'predicted chronological age'. There is an implicit assumption that the populational expectation of 'ECG-age' is the same as 'chronological age', so that one can use 'predicted chronological age' to approximate 'predicted ECG-age'.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that the model is trained on chronological age but the predicted value is named ECG-age to emphasize it is derived from ECG signal alone and captures aging effects; made nomenclature uniform throughout the paper and added explanatory paragraph in introduction.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper says 'This model indicates that participants with an estimated ECG-age of 8 or more years greater than the chronological age had higher mortality risk (HR 1.79, 95%CI 1.69-1.90; p<0.001).' However when I look at Table 2, I see ECG-age > age+8y has the hazard ratio 0.78. The text looks swapped from the main paper. I can't tell which one is correct.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors confirmed the table results were swapped and updated in the new version. Also added explanatory text about why patients with ECG-age more than 8 years greater than chronological age have lower average chronological age (survival selection effect).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is a difference between the ages of the two groups (supp table 1). What could be happening is that predictions are low for old people and high for young people, so the residuals separate the old and young people and would have the hazards in Table 2. This might persist even with age correction if the correction is linear. The discussion should have a limitation on the type of adjustment that was done. A non-linear correction with say a deep survival analysis model might reduce the observed relationship.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added limitation in discussion: 'one possible limitation of this analysis is that the relations considered in this second step are only the linear ones. Hence, taking into consideration nonlinear relations in this second step could possibly modify the observed relationship.'

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: What are the details of age groups for hold-out test set splitting? Validation in the methods part should be described more carefully. How was the data split?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors detailed an 80%-5%-15% split in the CODE cohort, with stratified sampling on age (70 uniformly spaced age groups, 16-85 years), and clarified only the first patient exam was used to prevent patient-level leakage.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: ECG signal-based — borderline imaging scope but uses tabular patient time-series. Solid extraction. Three reviewers across two rounds, all satisfied by round 2.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Tumor detection of CRC tissue is not a clinically relevant benchmark task. Compared with detection of prostate cancer in digitized histology images, CRC is very easily detectable even for non-experts. A pathologist only needs seconds to spot a typical CRC case. Tumor detection in CRC tissue has been long solved with near-perfect performance. The claims of the article are too strong.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors reframed the research goal as demonstrating a semi-supervised learning framework to reduce labeled data needs, not novel CRC detection; added two other cancer types (lung cancer and lymphoma) to demonstrate generalizability; toned down claims in abstract.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Generally, accurate detection of tumor tissue on patient level is much easier than on patch level. A very imperfect patch-based classifier can yield reasonable patient-level predictions. This is not adequately discussed in the article.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added detailed discussion about patch-level vs WSI/patient-level prediction trade-offs and false positive accumulation; described their clustering-based inference method to control false positives.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper does not adhere to the STARD-AI guidelines (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-020-0941-1).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors noted STARD-AI was not yet published at submission time but argued the paper meets STARD criteria; provided large CRC dataset and external validation cohorts; uploaded source code to GitHub.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Very important: there is no code available to assess the reproducibility of the work. The code should be made available to the reviewer with a well detailed README file.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors uploaded source code to GitHub at www.github.com/csu-bme/pathology_SSL with detailed README.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Considering the limited novelty in terms of application and methodology, I would suggest experiments with a wider range of diseases. Can the authors test three or four different diseases on whole slide images, and then conclude that semi-supervised deep learning is beneficial for general image classification based on whole slide images?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added experiments on lung cancer and lymphoma to demonstrate SSL applicability beyond CRC.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: We tested the known CNNs, such as VGG16, ResNET V1 and V2, Inception V1-V4, Mobilenet, etc., and found that InceptionV3 achieved most consistent results on many datasets. Please, do not use 'etc'. Be specific which ones were used. You state 'InceptionV3 achieved most consistent results on many datasets.' Since you've done those tests, please show the results in a (supp?) figure to support that observation.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified architecture choices and added details about hyper-parameter tuning and validation set selection in Supplementary A.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: Histopathology imaging — out of MLGG core scope. Two-round review with three reviewers. Most concerns resolved; STARD-AI compliance and patient-level accuracy concerns partially addressed.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The clustering results are not externally validated. At the very least it would be beneficial to show the same clustering results on ADNI1 and ADNI2 separately.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added 3 experiments: (i) train on ADNI2/GO, test on ADNI1; (ii) retrain on ADNI1, test on ADNI1; (iii) train and test on a larger iSTAGING dataset harmonized across seven studies. VBM results showed similar patterns.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: My main concern is that the method is arguably complicated and still lacks statistical verification. I would suggest a permutation experiment where the CN and CI status of the subjects are shuffled and the learning is repeated. This experiment would help to assess if the findings are significant and compute p-values.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors implemented the permutation experiment, showing failure to generate patterns using permuted data, establishing statistical significance of the four patterns.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The AD clusters identified by Smile-GAN seem to miss clusters of AD that have been identified previously. Of particular note is the lack of a limbic-predominant atrophy pattern, which has been identified at autopsy and in numerous structural MRI-based clustering studies.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added discussion mapping Smile-GAN patterns to previously identified subtypes (Limbic Predominant→P3, Hippocampal Sparing→P2, typical AD→mixed P2-P3); added supplementary section discussing why subcortical subtype was not distinctly identified.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There are multiple different analyses in different figures that likely use different subsets of the data. It would be very helpful if the authors describe in the legend of the figures the subset used in each analysis and the number of subjects used in each analysis. Could the authors briefly describe inclusion/exclusion criteria as well as diagnostic criteria of the different cohorts?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added subset details and N to each figure legend; added cohort inclusion/exclusion criteria, diagnostic criteria (NINCDS-ADRDA for ADNI), and references for ADNI/BLSA enrollment in Methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Z is Uniformly distributed. Does this imply that the subtypes need to be uniformly distributed? If this is the case, even approximately, does it means that the method would not be appropriate to identify rare patterns?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors implemented additional experiments testing robustness to unbalanced subgroups and non-uniform Z distribution, showing moderate imbalance is tolerated but very scarce patterns (<=10%) undermine clustering accuracy. Acknowledged limitation that rare/subtle atrophy patterns may not be distinctly learned.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: MRI imaging modality — out of MLGG core scope per CLAUDE.md. However, concerns about external validation, permutation testing, and cohort reporting are methodologically general.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: This is a single dataset study, whether the DL model is robust among different centers needs further validation. The random split of the training/testing sets make the training/testing sets have the same distribution in terms of follow-up and CT protocols. Namely, the DL model has seen part of the data distribution from all the involved centers. However, when applying the DL model in a completely different center that is not seen by the model, the CT scanning parameters can probably affect the results. It's important to validate the robustness of the DL model in CT images with various scanning parameters.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors documented 9 CT manufacturers, 81 manufacturer models, 65 reconstruction algorithms in VELOUR; performed reproducibility study with concordance coefficient 0.901 (95%CI 0.880-0.913) for ROI variation; noted similar C-Index in discovery (0.678) and test (0.649) cohorts despite parameter heterogeneity.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: When applying this method, different operators can generate different ROI. The size and location of the ROI can change if it is annotated by different user, how will this inter-operator variance affect the results?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors addressed inter-operator variance using RECIST-based standardized ROI selection and spatial augmentation; concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) for DL prediction score was 0.901 (95%CI 0.880-0.913) showing good reproducibility against ROI variation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Prognostic scores using sophisticated techniques such as DL need to be assessed in terms of their additional benefit relative to simple prognostic scores based on easily available clinical and pathological features familiar to clinicians. If interest focuses on predicting OS, one would ideally like to know: 1. What patient and tumor factors can reliably predict OS, 2. How much objective response assessed using RECIST adds to OS prediction 1, 3. How much ETS adds to OS prediction 2, 4. How much DL adds to OS prediction 3. In this paper one jumps right away to the last step, but without addressing the previous steps, the actual added value of the DL score remains unclear.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors built six other prognostic models (RECIST, TB, ETS, DL-BS, Size-Nomogram, DL-Nomogram) and showed incremental value of DL score; DL-Nomogram had best performance C-Index 0.649 vs ETS 0.627; new subsection 'Assessment of incremental value of DL-based method' added.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The statistical analysis part is really limited, while there is a lot to explain here. How were cut off chosen? how was performed internal validation? was p values adjusted to avoid overfitting? How Kaplan Meier curves compared?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified Youden Index used in tuning set (not test set) for cutoff selection; log-rank test for KM comparison; noted no need for p-value multiplicity adjustment since DL features were learned automatically.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Page 7, Statistical Analysis: descriptions are fuzzy and misleading. 'Hazard ratio (HR) and significance value were estimated by log-rank test'. The hazard ratio is not estimated by the logrank test, and the significance value (P-value) is not estimated at all. 'A landmark analysis correcting for bias was also performed'. What was the landmark chosen, and why was there bias? 'A p-value less than 0.001 was used to indicate statistical significance'. Why this low p-value. If to adjust for multiplicity, what drives the choice of 0.001?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors greatly expanded Statistical Analysis subsection clarifying log-rank test usage, landmark choice rationale, and significance threshold; corrected fuzzy descriptions.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: CT imaging — out of MLGG core scope. Strong concerns about incremental value and statistical methodology. All concerns resolved by round 2.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors must show both training and test set errors across all 20 splits training/test set samples. Ideally, the final model should be evaluated on a completely independent/withheld set of patients.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors performed repeated (n=20) 5-fold cross-validation with results in revised Fig. 4b and new Supplementary Fig. 10; acknowledged no external dataset available and committed to recruit independent cohort in future.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors use a mixed cohort of early stage lung cancer patients comprising different tumor types. Patients with distinct tumor types (eg Lung Adeno vs. Squamous) could have substantially different expected/baseline treatment outcomes. Furthermore, the authors note that Lung Adenocarcinoma tumors have noticeably lower ctDNA detection frequency. Overall, these factors could confound the different types of survival analysis conducted throughout the paper.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors controlled for tumor types in multivariate Cox model showing ctDNA status remained significant; performed survival analysis stratified by AD vs SqCC (added Supplementary Fig. 5); reached consistent conclusions.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It is not clear if the authors are sharing code and data ensuring reproducible research. The authors should share all code and data that reproduces figures and key survival analysis in this manuscript. The raw targeted sequencing data for both tumor and liquid biopsies should also be shared.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors shared source data file for figures, code on GitHub at cancer-oncogenomics/ctDNA-dynamic-prediction-lung-cancer; specific mutations in Supplementary Table 2; raw sequencing data restricted due to Human Genetic Resources Administration of China regulations but available upon request after acceptance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Variant calling without matched normals: In the mutation calling part (for both tumor and plasma samples), it seems the author did not sequence the matched buffy coat? It has been demonstrated the sequencing of matched cfDNA-white blood cell is important for accurate variant interpretation in the presence of Somatic Hematopoesis (Razavi et al., Nature Medicine, 2019).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified they did sequence white blood cells as normal controls to identify germline variants and somatic hematopoiesis-related mutations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The simple Cox model (landmark) appear to have comparable or lower prediction error than the joint model. Whats the advantage of the joint model then?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors used Monte Carlo simulation instead of first-order estimator for AUROC/prediction error; updated comparison showing joint model AUROC significantly higher; added calibration via reliability diagrams using Hosmer-Lemeshow C-statistics demonstrating better agreement (smaller C-statistic values) for joint model.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I think the methodology needs to be presented with vastly more details, as although the results are quite encouraging, it is troublesome that so many patients with metastasis do not have detectable ctDNA. However, this could also simply reflect interpretation of too few mutation targets per patient/sample, but this needs to be discussed. And that a handful of patients have no recurrence despite having detectable ctDNA.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors expanded methodology details, addressed ctDNA detection sensitivity, and discussed discrepant cases.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: ctDNA + clinical — borderline genomic/clinical. Two reviewers, two rounds. External validation gap acknowledged as future work.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Major issue: The use of any blood culture as a proxy for infection is questionable, at least in the way it is presented here. The citation from which it seems to get evidence is not published nor replicated while other longitudinal studies found frequent contamination in blood cultures in CLL (Kjellander et al. Ann Hematol 2016). This needs to be discussed more profoundly or maybe even completely revised.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors provided detailed justification: blood culture drawn (irrespective of result) used as proxy for clinical infection per Danish guidelines; cited multiple references supporting this proxy use; added clarification in Methods and Discussion that this proxy holds prognostic and learnable information per their data-driven results showing significantly higher recall than CLL-IPI.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why was the time-point 0 shifted to 3 months post-diagnosis when the whole evaluation is using methods for incorporation of missing data?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained the 3-month time-point allows critical diagnostic tests (IGHV status, FISH, TP53) to be available; for the external German cohort, time-point 0 varied 0-1 year post-diagnosis; rationale was to remove patients (n=373) already identified by clinicians as needing early treatment, avoiding positive bias.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Discussion of selection bias is lacking.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added discussion that predictions on entire test cohort (n=646) represent the Danish CLL population (98% registry coverage); acknowledged Danish cohort represents more indolent population; noted patients with incomplete diagnostic work-up fare worse, affecting subset with full CLL-IPI.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Bag of words has two major issues which are not discussed: a) it has the curse of dimensionality issue as the total dimension is the vocabulary size. It can easily over-fit your model. The limited remedy is to use some well-known dimensionality reduction technique to your input data. b) Bag of words representation doesn't consider the semantic relation between words. Generally, the neighbor words in a sentence should be useful for predicting your target word.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified BOW dimensions were reduced (pathology BOW from 1572 to 153, diagnosis BOW from 3386 to 216); applied multiple feature selection methods (XGBoost FS, RF FS, ExtraTrees FS, ANOVA F-Value FS) so no base-learner trained on >150 features. Argued BOW for diagnostic coding has no spatial neighbors but acknowledged semantic similarity could be modeled with embeddings given larger cohorts.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Despite moderate improvement in PR-AUC vs IPI, results remain modest while confidence intervals are overlapping, and results for the external german cohort are quite modest and differences are smaller. These limitations in practical relevance need to be critically discussed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors elaborated on overlapping CIs being expected due to bootstrap from single test set and binomial-vs-MCC distribution differences; used Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired bootstrap comparison; added Table showing MCC variability in bootstrap; explained German cohort context (half high-risk patients removed for early treatment in CLL7 arm).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors say they used the SHAP framework. Why did they not use typical machine learning methods for feature ranking, such as Random Forests, Support Vector Machine with radial Gaussian kernel, One Rule? Relying completely on one method (SHAP, in this case), is never a good idea. The authors should use multiple methods.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified SHAP was used for post-learning unification across 28 base-learners due to consistency property and local interpretability needs; added univariate techniques (Student's t-test, ANOVA F-Value, Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis) in Supplementary Tables 4-6 to confirm risk factors.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors claim they predict 'infection or CLL treatment', but this expression is confusing. What does it mean? Is an infection the same thing of a CLL treatment? Are they predicting both? Why are these two concepts treated in the same way?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained the composite outcome rationale: a high-risk patient is one who initiates treatment OR experiences infection OR both within 2 years; aligned with clinical observation that infection is leading mortality cause in CLL; modeled synergy between outcomes via shared signal and remodeled main figure for clarity.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors say their tool handles efficiently missing data, but they do not explain how.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added new Online Methods section 'Handling of Missing Data' describing multi-level approach: feature-level (one-hot encoded missingness indicators), base-learner level (XGBoost native handling, median imputation for others), ensemble level (diverse base-learners compensate for missing patterns).

papers_processed.extraction_notes: Core MLGG-scope paper (EHR tabular, binary classification, retrospective CLL cohort). Rich set of substantive concerns covering label definition, selection bias, missingness, feature engineering, calibration, interpretability. Both reviewers fully satisfied by round 2.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It is not clear why you did not just add the clinical features directly to the neural network, potentially just before the last layer. It would be good to compare the performance of such an architecture with the one proposed here.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors compared their model (Resnet50 + SVM) against Resnet50_concatenate (clinical features in last FC layer), Resnet101, Inception v3, vgg19; their proposed model achieved highest AUC (0.915) and accuracy (0.82) with lowest memory (98 Mb).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Were these consecutive lesions? If not, exactly who was recruited and why? It is not believable that no patient had multiple lesions, in my experience 10-20% of breast cancer patients have multifocal disease on US and 2% have bilateral disease, please explain, if multifocal disease was excluded please state, if the largest lesion only was included please state. If so this needs discussion.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified consecutive breast lesions were enrolled; patients with multifocal and bilateral disease were excluded due to ambiguity in which lesion drives ALN metastasis; stated this exclusion in Methods and discussed in limitations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In patients with a pre-operative diagnosis of axillary metastases (fna or core) how good was prediction of nodal burden at surgery? Especially those who had ANC? This is a crucial clinical question.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors used different cut-offs of positive ALNs to predict nodal burden: disease-free (N0), low burden (N+1-2), heavy burden (N+≥3); reported separately in revised manuscript.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Reporting the results of the training dataset (instead of a completely independent dataset) leads to overly optimistic assessment of the performance. The training and validation can be moved to the supplement if necessary but it is imperative that the test performance is reported in the main manuscript. Since you performed boot-strap analysis, please provide those confidence intervals, not just point estimates for the results.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors changed Tables 1, 3, 4 to include test set results and added 95% confidence intervals throughout revised manuscript.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The results of the visualization are very qualitative. Can you quantify them?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added a color bar ranging 0 to 1 for pseudo colors and quantitative analysis in revised figure.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: What was the inter-rater agreement? Did you pre-process your images (besides cropping)? Normalize? Please provide full details of the preprocessing step.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors reported Kappa 0.933 (inter-observer) and 1.0 (intra-observer) for axillary US assessment; added preprocessing details (ROIs resized to 224x224 pixels, normalized by subtracting mean and dividing by std).

papers_processed.extraction_notes: Ultrasound imaging + clinical — borderline imaging scope. Three rounds with two reviewers. Strong concern about training set vs test set reporting (R1 round 2) which was resolved.
